P.w: Opened in 2001 as the first Universal Studios park in Asia; one of Japan's most visited theme parks, with areas including The Wizarding World of Harry Potter and Super Nintendo World.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Super Nintendo World (the world's first, 2021) — Mario Kart, Donkey Kong Country and Nintendo characters, plus Harry Potter, Minions and seasonal anime collabs · theme park

P.ad: 1-1-10 Kaigan-dori, Minato-ku, Osaka (Tempozan Harbor Village), Japan
P.w: One of Japan's largest aquariums, built around a 5,400-ton central Pacific tank holding a whale shark, with exhibits themed on the Pacific Rim.

P.ad: Tempozan Harbor Village, 1-1-10 Kaigan-dori, Minato-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: A 112.5 m Ferris wheel beside Kaiyūkan in Tempozan Harbor Village, with a roughly 15-minute ride over Osaka Bay and the city skyline.

P.ad: Osaka Prefectural Government Sakishima Building, 1-14-16 Nanko-kita, Suminoe-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: Observation deck 252 m up atop the Sakishima building (completed 1995), giving a 360-degree panorama of Osaka Bay; known for night views.
Head shrine of over two thousand Sumiyoshi shrines across Japan, protecting travellers and sailors; its four main halls face west in the ancient Sumiyoshi-zukuri style.

P.n: Mozu Kofun Group — Daisen Kofun (Emperor Nintoku's Tomb)
P.w: Cluster of 5th-century keyhole tombs in Sakai, UNESCO World Heritage (2019) with the Furuichi group; Daisen Kofun, attributed to Emperor Nintoku, is the largest grave in the world by area (~840 m with moats). The mound itself is off-limits.

P.ad: Daisen Park, 2 Mozu Yugumo-cho, Sakai-ku, Sakai, Osaka, Japan
P.w: Museum in Daisen Park tracing the history of the port town of Sakai, starting with the kofun tombs and artifacts excavated from them.

P.n: Expo '70 Commemorative Park & Tower of the Sun
P.w: Vast park on the grounds of the 1970 Japan World Exposition, the first in Asia; Tarō Okamoto's 70 m Tower of the Sun stands over the main entrance as its icon.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Taro Okamoto's Tower of the Sun — a pop-art icon of Expo '70 and a key motif of Naoki Urasawa's manga 20th Century Boys · park / monument

P.w: Forested valley just north of Osaka with a roughly 3 km riverside trail from Hankyu Minoo Station to the 33 m Minoo Waterfall; famous for autumn colours.
Mountain temple above Minoh known as the temple of victory, its grounds dotted with thousands of small red daruma dolls left by wishers.

P.ad: 10-1 Senri Expo Park, Suita, Osaka, Japan
P.w: One of the world's largest ethnology museums, inside the Expo '70 Commemorative Park, with a huge exhibition of everyday artifacts from cultures around the world.
Hands-on museum in Ikeda, birthplace of instant ramen (Momofuku Ando, 1958); at My Cup Noodles Factory visitors design a cup and pick their own soup and toppings.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Momofuku Ando instant-ramen pop culture — where Chicken Ramen (1958) was invented · museum

P.w: Widely considered Japan's finest surviving feudal castle — the white 'White Heron' keep is a National Treasure and a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1993).
Hillside district where foreign merchants and diplomats settled after Kobe port opened in the 19th century; dozens of Western-style mansions (ijinkan) survive, many open as museums.
Waterfront park on reclaimed land in Kobe's port, home to the red 108 m Kobe Port Tower (1963), the Kobe Maritime Museum and the Earthquake Memorial.
Shopping and entertainment waterfront between JR Kobe Station and the port, popular at night for its harbour views.

P.ad: Sakaemachi-dori / Motomachi-dori, Chuo-ku, Kobe, Hyogo, Japan
P.w: The biggest Chinatown in western Japan, packed with more than 100 shops and restaurants and street-food stalls.
One of Japan's oldest shrines, said to be founded in the 3rd century by Empress Jingū; the name Kobe derives from 'Kanbe', the families who served it.
One of Japan's three most famous hot springs, over Mount Rokko from central Kobe; known for its iron-rich 'kinsen' gold and clear 'ginsen' silver waters, explorable on foot.
Four waterfalls (the tallest, Ontaki, 43 m) a short walk from Shin-Kobe Station; the Nunobiki Ropeway climbs above them to one of Japan's largest herb gardens.
The 931 m high point of the Rokko range behind Kobe, with panoramic views over Kobe and Osaka, especially at sunset and night.
Spanning the Akashi Strait to Awaji Island, it was long the world's longest suspension bridge (central span 1,991 m).

P.ad: Nada-gogo, Higashinada-ku / Nada-ku, Kobe, Hyogo, Japan
P.w: Japan's top sake-producing district; several breweries run shops, tasting rooms and brewing museums open to the public.
Kōbō Daishi's mausoleum at the end of a cemetery path through ancient cedars lined with over 200,000 graves; part of the UNESCO 'Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range'.
Head temple of Shingon Buddhism on Mount Kōya, founded by Kōbō Daishi in the 9th century; within the Kii Mountains UNESCO site.
Reconstructed castle keep on a hill in central Wakayama with free Nishinomaru garden and the maple-filled Momijidani garden and covered wooden bridge.
Castle-town keep (burned 1827, rebuilt 1954) halfway between Osaka and Wakayama, with 360-degree views over Osaka Bay; the town is famous for the Danjiri float festival.
Bayfront district one stop from Kansai Airport with the 256 m SiS Rinku Tower (Rinku Gate Tower Building), Rinku Premium Outlets (200+ shops) and Aeon Mall.

P.n: Kansai Airport Observation Hall Sky View
P.w: Observation hall at Kansai International Airport with 360-degree runway views, an aviation shop and the Sky Museum.
Japan's oldest operating amusement park ('Hira-Par'), with around 40 attractions including the ~80 m Sky Walker Ferris wheel.
6th-century keyhole mound believed to be the true tomb of Emperor Keitai; unusually open to walk on, with replica haniwa on display and the Imashirozuka Ancient History Museum next door.

About a quarter of Taishō Ward's residents have Okinawan roots, descendants of WWI-era migrant textile workers; Okinawan restaurants and shops cluster near JR Taisho Station and along the Hirao shopping street.
Nine walled Edo-style gardens built in 1992 on the site of former samurai residences beside Himeji Castle's west moat.

P.n: Umeda Sky Building — Kuchū Teien Floating Garden Observatory
P.ad: Umeda Sky Building, northwest of JR Osaka Station, Kita-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: The 173 m twin-tower skyscraper (1993) joined at the top by the open-air Floating Garden observation deck — 360° views over Osaka, open till 22:30.
Temma's shrine to Sugawara no Michizane, god of learning, at the head of Tenjinbashi-suji; home of the Tenjin Matsuri.
The national mint where Japan's coins are struck; famous for opening its riverside avenue of cherry trees to the public each spring.

P.ad: HEP Five, east of Hankyu Umeda, Kita-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: A red Ferris wheel bursting from the roof of the HEP shopping complex in Umeda — 106 m high, with views over Kita.
Hideyoshi's 1583 castle, rebuilt in 1931 — the main keep (a museum with a top-floor lookout) rises from stone walls and moats in a vast park famous for plum and cherry blossom.
The canal-side heart of kuidaore Osaka: neon, mechanised signs (the Glico Running Man, the Kani Doraku crab) and street food that barely closes.
"Osaka's Kitchen": a several-hundred-metre covered arcade of fishmongers, butchers, greengrocers and grill-it-on-the-spot stalls.
Osaka's premier shopping street — a ~600 m covered arcade mixing chain stores, boutiques and department stores, running north from Dōtonbori.
Osaka's answer to Harajuku: thrift stores, cafes and youth fashion around Triangle Park, west of Mido-suji.
The 'New World' district built after the 1903 Expo — half Paris, half Coney Island — around Tsūtenkaku, the 103 m tower rebuilt in 1956; the home of Osaka kushikatsu.
Founded by Prince Shōtoku in 593 — one of Japan's oldest temples and the first built by the state, with its five-storey pagoda on the classic straight-line layout.

P.ad: Tennōji Park, Chausuyamacho, Tennoji-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: Osaka's city zoo (1915) in Tennōji Park, below Tsūtenkaku.

P.n: Osaka City Museum of Fine Arts
P.ad: Tennōji Park, Chausuyamacho, Tennoji-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: The 1936 municipal art museum in Tennōji Park, with Keitakuen garden behind it.
Opened 2001 in a tower beside NHK Osaka, across from the castle: large-scale models chronicle the city from its days as Japan's first capital to the early Shōwa era, with views over the castle park.
Contemporary Japanese and international art on two underground floors of Nakanoshima; the 2007 building's entrance structure is designed to evoke growing bamboo.
Hands-on science museum and planetarium on Nakanoshima, next to the National Museum of Art.
The city art museum that opened on Nakanoshima in February 2022 — modern and contemporary art and design, part of the island's museum cluster.
Claimed as Japan's longest covered shopping street — 2.6 km of shops and eateries running north from the Tenmangū approach.

A moss-covered Fudō Myōō statue that worshippers splash with water, beside two 80 m stone-paved alleys of old kappo counters, bars and okonomiyaki shops — the setting of Oda Sakunosuke's 'Meoto Zenzai'.
Osaka's Akihabara: electronics, anime, games and maid cafés along Sakaisuji in Nipponbashi.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Kansai's otaku district — Nipponbashi Ota Road, Animate, Mandarake and Jungle for anime, manga, figures and retro games · electronics & otaku district

P.w: Osaka's grown-up entertainment quarter just south of Osaka Station — hundreds of restaurants, hostess bars and counters.
A pocket of pre-war row houses east of Umeda whose narrow lanes are now full of cafés, craft shops and vintage stores.
Osaka's oldest tutelary shrine, an Engishiki-listed great shrine to the land deities Ikushima and Tarushima, on the Uemachi ridge near Tanimachi 9-chōme.

P.ad: Osaka Castle Park, Chuo-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: Shrine inside Osaka Castle Park enshrining Toyotomi Hideyoshi, Hideyori and Hidenaga as deities of success — a branch of Kyoto's Toyokuni Shrine.
Jon Jerde's 2003 mall on the old Osaka Stadium site, shaped like a canyon of rock strata, with ~70,000 plants on its terraced rooftop Parks Garden.
Japan's largest Koreatown: about 150 grocers, kimchi and chijimi stalls, restaurants and hanbok shops along a 300 m shopping street in Ikuno, a short walk from Tsuruhashi's yakiniku alleys.
The nation's most prestigious stage for bunraku, Osaka's own puppet theatre — runs of about three weeks in January, April, June, July/August and November.
The Umekita redevelopment beside JR Osaka Station — a large urban park with new towers opening in stages through spring 2027, next to the Grand Front Osaka complex.
Open lawns and reconstructed platform bases across from Osaka Castle Park marking the 7th–8th-century imperial palace of Naniwa-kyō, when Osaka was Japan's capital.
The ~300 m skyscraper that opened in 2014 — department store, hotel, art museum and the Harukas 300 observation deck with panoramic views across Osaka.

P.ad: Tennōji Park, Chausuyamacho, Tennoji-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: A 19,800 m² strolling pond garden behind the city art museum, designed by tea master Kizu Issai and built by Ogawa Jihei VII (of Heian Shrine and Murin-an fame); entry is just ¥150.
The park holding the zoo, greenhouse, art museum and Keitakuen, fronted by 'Tenshiba' — a Good Design Award-winning lawn with cafés a short walk from Tennōji Station.
Some 800 stalls in the warren beside Tsuruhashi Station — yakiniku, kimchi and Korean groceries, fresh fish and offal hot-pots; the smell of grilling meat greets you on the platform.

P.n: Ebisubashi & the Glico Running Man sign
P.ad: Ebisubashi bridge, Dōtonbori, Chuo-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: The bridge over the Dōtonbori canal where everyone poses with the Glico Running Man — the neon heart of Minami's mechanised signs.

Famous for its 12 m-high lion-head stage, whose gaping mouth swallows bad luck and brings victory in competition; the shrine was rebuilt after the 1945 air raids and keeps an intangible-folk-culture tug-of-war rite.
Yoshimoto's 858-seat 'hall of laughter', Japan's largest comedy theatre — Yoshimoto Shinkigeki, manzai and rakugo 365 days a year.
Shinsekai's 130 m covered alley of kushikatsu and doteyaki counters and old game parlours, running south toward Dōbutsuen-mae.
A 150 m arcade of professional kitchen-supply shops — knives, plastic food samples, lanterns, signs and tableware — three minutes from Namba Station.

P.n: LUCUA Characters World — Pokémon Center Osaka & Nintendo OSAKA
P.ad: LUCUA SOUTH 10–13F (South Gate Building), JR Osaka Station, Umeda, Kita-ku, Osaka
P.w: Osaka's answer to Tokyo's Character Street: LUCUA SOUTH opened 5 April 2026 and gathered Pokémon Center Osaka, Nintendo OSAKA and the ONE PIECE Mugiwara Store (moved from Daimaru Umeda) on its top floors, growing to 30+ character shops (Sanrio, Square Enix, Minecraft) by autumn 2026.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Pokémon · Nintendo (Mario, Zelda, Splatoon) · One Piece — Kansai's biggest official character-store cluster, the Pokémon Center and Nintendo flagship stores of western Japan · character shops, pop culture

P.w: Memorial museum to the 'God of Manga' (Astro Boy, Black Jack, Phoenix) in Takarazuka, the town where he grew up — permanent display of his life and work plus rotating exhibitions, ~30 min by train from Osaka. Note: special long closure 1 Dec 2026 – 4 Mar 2027.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Osamu Tezuka (Astro Boy / Tetsuwan Atom, Black Jack, Princess Knight) — the founding father of modern manga and TV anime, in his hometown · museum

P.ad: Wakamatsu Park, Wakamatsu-chō, Nagata-ku, Kobe, Hyōgo
P.w: A full-scale 18 m steel Tetsujin-28 robot raised in Wakamatsu Park by the KOBE Tetsujin Project as a symbol of recovery from the 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake; Nagata was creator Mitsuteru Yokoyama's hometown. Short walk from Shin-Nagata Station.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Tetsujin 28-go (Gigantor) by Mitsuteru Yokoyama — a life-size giant robot honouring the Kobe-born manga pioneer and the earthquake recovery · statue, monument

P.w: Kansai's first Anpanman Children's Museum (2013) at Kobe Harborland: hands-on play museum with daily stage shows and an Anpanman bakery and shop in a free-entry mall — the go-to stop for families with small children.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Soreike! Anpanman (Takashi Yanase) — Japan's best-loved preschool anime hero, with his own bakery-themed museum · museum, family

P.ad: Near JR Ōtori Station, Sakai, Osaka, Japan
P.w: Ichinomiya (first shrine) of old Izumi Province, c. 1,900 years old, enshrining Yamato Takeru; a five-minute walk from JR Ōtori Station.
Ancient Kōyasan Shingon temple (founded 701, restored by Kūkai 815) holding the National Treasure Nyoirin Kannon and Kondō hall; plum, cherry and autumn-leaf spot.
Mountain temple patronised by Toyotomi Hideyoshi (his letter survives here), with National Treasure Buddhist statues shown in autumn special exhibitions.

P.n: Chikatsu Asuka Museum (大阪府立近つ飛鳥博物館)
P.w: Tadao Ando's stepped kofun-shaped museum of Japan's burial-mound age, set in the Chikatsu Asuka Fudoki-no-Oka tomb park.

P.ad: In front of Hamadera Ekimae / Hamadera-kōen Station, Sakai & Takaishi, Osaka, Japan
P.w: One of the prefecture's oldest parks (1873), a seaside pine grove at the end of the Hankai tram; the Tatsuno Kingo-office Hamadera-kōen station building is a rare Meiji survivor.
Museum of the Kishiwada Danjiri Matsuri — the September festival where carved wooden floats are hauled at a run round street corners.
Hundertwasser-designed waste plant on an artificial island — red, black and white walls, a golden onion tower and roof greenery; free guided interior tours by reservation.

P.ad: Tempozan Park, Chikkō, Minato-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: 'Japan's lowest mountain' — a 4.5 m summit marker inside a harbourside park with a hidden cherry-blossom grove and an Emperor Meiji monument; 7 min from Osakakō Station.

P.ad: Tempozan Harbor Village, 1 Kaigan-dōri, Minato-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: The harbour mall at the heart of Tempozan Harbor Village, beside the Ferris wheel and Kaiyūkan; inside are the retro Shōwa food alley Naniwa Kuishinbo Yokochō and LEGOLAND Discovery Center Osaka.
Kawachi's ichinomiya at the foot of the Ikoma range, said to date back 2,600+ years; famous for its plum grove and the 23 December 'laughing ritual' (Owarai Shinji).

P.n: Ishikiri Tsurugiya Shrine (石切劔箭神社)
P.w: 'Ishikiri-san', the god of swellings — nationally known for the ohyakudo-mairi, worshippers circling between the stones and the hall, and a fortune-teller-lined approach street.
Japan's largest greenhouse botanical garden, built as Osaka's pavilion for Expo '90 in Tsurumi Ryokuchi Park — ~15,000 plants of 5,500 species.
Birthplace of Japanese malt whisky (built 1923): whisky museum, paid tastings and a lottery-entry production tour; 10 min walk from JR Yamazaki / Hankyu Ōyamazaki.

P.n: Open-Air Museum of Old Japanese Farmhouses (日本民家集落博物館)
P.w: Japan's first open-air museum (1956), in Hattori Ryokuchi Park: 11 relocated 17th-19th-century folk houses from Iwate to Amami Ōshima.
En no Gyōja-founded temple on the Minoo Falls trail, home to one of Japan's four great Benzaiten and billed as the birthplace of the Japanese lottery; 15 min walk from Hankyu Minoh.
Shrine to Ame-no-Iwafune, a 12 m boat-shaped boulder up the Amanogawa valley; the 'iwa-kuguri' rock-cave crawl beneath the giant stones is open to visitors.

P.n: Hirakatashuku Kagiya Museum (枚方宿鍵屋資料館)
P.w: Edo-period riverside inn where travellers waited for the Fushimi-Osaka riverboats on the Kyō-kaidō post town; a cultural property, opened as a museum in 2001.

P.n: Engyō-ji (Mount Shosha, 書写山圓教寺)
P.w: Atmospheric 1,000-year-old mountain temple complex 30 min from Himeji by bus and ropeway; the Mitsunodō halls were a set for The Last Samurai.
Kōyasan's central temple complex, founded where Kūkai found his thrown sankosho in a pine; dominated by the Kondō hall and the vermilion Konpon Daitō pagoda.

P.n: Furuichi Kofun Group — Konda Gobyōyama Kofun (誉田御廟山古墳)
P.w: The second-largest keyhole tomb in Japan (attributed to Emperor Ōjin), heart of the Furuichi half of the UNESCO Mozu-Furuichi kofun group, next to Konda Hachimangū near Kintetsu Furuichi Station.

P.ad: Kongō range, Chihaya-Akasaka village, Osaka / Nara border, Japan
P.w: Osaka's highest peak (1,125 m) and the prefecture's favourite hike — ropeway, summit shrine and frosted-tree winter scenery in the Kongō-Ikoma-Kisen Quasi-National Park.

P.ad: Senri Banpaku Kōen, Suita, Osaka, Japan
P.w: Entertainment complex beside Expo '70 Park: the Kaiyūkan team's 'living museum' NIFREL and Japan's tallest Ferris wheel, plus a large mall.

P.n: Hoshida Park — Hoshi no Buranko suspension bridge (星のブランコ)
P.ad: Osaka Prefectural Forest Hoshida Park, Katano, Osaka, Japan
P.w: Japan's largest wooden pedestrian suspension bridge, the 'Star Swing', strung across a valley of the Tanabata-legend Amanogawa forest above Katano.

P.n: Hanazono Rugby Stadium (東大阪市花園ラグビー場)
P.w: Japan's oldest rugby-only stadium (1929), the 'holy ground' of the national high-school tournament and a 2019 Rugby World Cup venue; free Hanazono Rugby Museum on match days.

P.n: Fujita Museum of Art (藤田美術館)
P.w: Meiji magnate Fujita Denzaburō's collection of ~2,000 Asian artworks — 9 National Treasures (incl. a yōhen tenmoku tea bowl) and 53 Important Cultural Properties — in a rebuilt gallery by Kyōbashi.

P.n: Shiba Ryōtarō Memorial Museum (司馬遼太郎記念館)
P.w: The historical novelist's house and study beside a Tadao Ando library hall whose 11 m wall of shelves holds part of his 60,000-book collection.

P.n: Panasonic Museum (Kōnosuke Matsushita History Museum, Kadoma)
P.w: Free museum at Panasonic's Kadoma home: founder Matsushita Kōnosuke's story, the 'Monozukuri-ism' hall of landmark home appliances, and Sakura Square.

P.n: Kyocera Dome Osaka (京セラドーム大阪)
P.w: Kansai's largest indoor stadium (36,220 seats for baseball), home of the Orix Buffaloes and Osaka's big-concert dome; Tugboat Taishō waterfront food-and-art strip is a short walk away.

P.ad: Chikkō Red Brick Warehouse, Chikkō, Minato-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: Classic-car museum of about 80 landmark cars (e.g. a 1900-1950 Rolls-Royce Phantom II era line-up) inside the 1923 Chikkō red-brick port warehouse near Tempozan.

P.n: Osaka Maishima Seaside Park (大阪まいしまシーサイドパーク)
P.w: Seasonal flower park on Maishima island (formerly the Maishima Lily Garden): about a million nemophila against the bay in April, lilies in early summer.

P.n: Ikeda Castle Ruins Park (池田城跡公園)
P.w: Park (2000) on the site of the Ikeda clan's castle: stroll garden with a central pond, tea room and a lookout tower with views to Takarazuka, Osaka and Kobe.

P.n: Satsukiyama Park & Zoo (五月山公園・五月山動物園)
P.w: Ikeda's hillside park for spring cherry blossom and autumn leaves; at its foot the free Satsukiyama Zoo, Japan's second-smallest, famous for its wombats.

P.n: Itsuō Art Museum & Kobayashi Ichizō Memorial Hall (逸翁美術館)
P.w: Collection of Hankyu/Takarazuka founder Kobayashi Ichizō (pen-name Itsuō) — early-modern paintings and tea ceramics — beside his Gazoku Sansō residence, now the memorial hall.

P.n: Kobe Earthquake Memorial Museum (人と防災未来センター)
P.ad: HAT Kobe, Chūō-ku, Kobe, Hyōgo, Japan
P.w: Memorial museum of the 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake (opened 2002): a large-screen recreation of the quake, a recovery documentary and hands-on disaster-prevention exhibits.
Early-20th-century landscape garden of former Kobe mayor Kodera Kenkichi, public since 1941, with a relocated Western-style residence and boathouse; 300 yen, closed Thursdays.

P.n: Kobe City Museum (神戸市立博物館)
P.ad: Old Settlement (Kyūkyoryūchi), Chūō-ku, Kobe, Hyōgo, Japan
P.w: Archaeology and one of the world's largest collections of Namban art — Japanese painting from the first contact with Western ships in the 1500s — in a former bank in the old foreign settlement.

P.n: Osaka Museum of Housing and Living (大阪くらしの今昔館)
P.w: Walk-through, life-size reconstruction of an Edo-period Osaka merchant townscape on the upper floors of a building at the north end of Tenjinbashi-suji. Closed for renovation until 5 January 2027 (japan-guide e4024) — check before visiting.

P.n: Daisen Park Japanese Garden (大仙公園日本庭園)
P.ad: Daisen Park, Sakai-ku, Sakai, Osaka, Japan
P.w: 26,000 m² stroll garden of hill, forest and spring evoking medieval Sakai, inside Daisen Park beside Emperor Nintoku's tomb; matcha at the Shinan teahouse; 5 min from JR Mozu.

P.n: Temma Tenjin Hanjo Tei (天満天神繁昌亭, rakugo theatre)
P.w: Osaka's dedicated rakugo hall (yose) beside Osaka Tenmangū — the home stage of Kamigata comic storytelling, with daily shows.

P.ad: Universal Studios Japan, 2-1-33 Sakurajima, Konohana-ku, Osaka
P.w: The world's first Super Nintendo World opened inside USJ on 18 March 2021 (Mario Kart: Koopa's Challenge, Yoshi's Adventure); the Donkey Kong Country expansion (Mine Cart Madness) opened 11 Dec 2024 and grew the land by ~70%. Timed-entry via the USJ app on busy days.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Nintendo — Super Mario & Donkey Kong; the first Nintendo theme-park land anywhere, built in Osaka · theme-park land

P.ad: Hyōgo Prefectural Awaji Shima Park, Awaji, Hyōgo
P.w: Anime theme park opened 15 July 2017 inside Awaji Shima Park: Naruto & Boruto, Dragon Quest, Crayon Shin-chan, SPY×FAMILY attractions and a life-size Shin Godzilla you zip-line into (Godzilla Interception Operation, 2020). Park entry free; attractions ~¥2,000–6,000. ~90 min by highway bus from Osaka.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Naruto · Godzilla · Dragon Quest · Crayon Shin-chan — Kansai's only multi-franchise anime theme park · anime theme park

P.w: Kitty-head-shaped Sanrio complex on the Seto Inland Sea: an underwater Hello Kitty princess digital-art show plus two restaurants serving on Kitty tableware; the Hello Kitty Show Box (live musical lunch) is a short bus ride away.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Sanrio — Hello Kitty; the Kansai counterpart to Tokyo's Puroland · character attraction

P.w: Home stage of the all-female Takarazuka Revue. Osamu Tezuka grew up nearby and his mother took him here; the Revue's male-role stars, costumes and big sparkling eyes shaped Princess Knight and his whole art style. Pair with the Tezuka Manga Museum a short walk away.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Osamu Tezuka — Princess Knight (Ribbon no Kishi) was directly inspired by the Takarazuka Revue · theatre

P.n: Haruhi Suzumiya pilgrimage — Kissa-ya Dream (珈琲屋ドリーム), Nishinomiya
P.ad: Kōfūen 1-chōme, Nishinomiya, Hyōgo (about 1 min from Nishinomiya-Kitaguchi Station)
P.w: Author Nagaru Tanigawa is from Nishinomiya and the SOS Brigade's café is this real kissaten; Nishinomiya was named an Anime Tourism 88 pilgrimage site (2019 edition) with plaques at the café and the Nomura Securities branch. Fans hang Tanabata decorations here every summer.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — The Melancholy of Haruhi Suzumiya — the SOS Brigade's meeting café; Nishinomiya = Anime Tourism 88 seichi (2019) · anime pilgrimage site

P.n: Niteko Pond & Grave of the Fireflies memorial (Nishinomiya)
P.w: The pond and hillside where Seita and Setsuko shelter in Akiyuki Nosaka's story (Ghibli film 1988); a 'Grave of the Fireflies' memorial stone was erected in June 2020 in the adjoining Nishinomiya earthquake memorial park. Cherry blossoms in spring.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Grave of the Fireflies (Studio Ghibli, Isao Takahata) — the real setting of the siblings' pond-side shelter · anime pilgrimage site

P.w: Neo-Renaissance red-brick hall completed 1918 with a donation from stockbroker Einosuke Iwamoto (design Tatsuno Kingo & Okada Shin'ichirō); restored 1999–2002 and designated an Important Cultural Property in 2002. Free basement history exhibit.

1,300-year-old Umeda shrine named for Sugawara no Michizane's dew-and-tears poem; nicknamed after Ohatsu, heroine of Chikamatsu's 1703 'Love Suicides at Sonezaki', set in its grove — now a matchmaking power spot.

Temple founded by Gyōki in 744; its wooden main hall (rebuilt 1808) miraculously survived the WWII air raids amid the Minami neon. Appears in Chikamatsu's Sonezaki Shinjū and the rakugo story 'Mameda'.

CLOSED: Dōtonbori's neo-Renaissance theatre (opened 1923 as a cinema, kabuki/stage house since 1997) gave its final performance, the 'Onagori Gogatsu Ōkabuki', on 26 May 2026 after 103 years; Shochiku plans to demolish the ageing building. Facade-only now — no shows.

P.ad: Namba 1-chōme (corner lot west of Hōzen-ji), Chūō-ku, Osaka
P.w: The only museum anywhere with a permanent display of Kamigata (Osaka-Kyoto) ukiyo-e — realistic kabuki-actor prints of stars like Nakamura Utaemon III, ~30 works over four small floors, plus print-making classes (reservation). Free with the Osaka Amazing Pass.

P.ad: Minami-Horie, Nishi-ku, Osaka (3 min from Yotsubashi Station)
P.w: 800 m street that began as an Edo-era furniture town; now indie Japanese labels, vintage furniture and clothes, and open-air cafés beside old craftsman furniture shops. Time Out ranked it the world's second-coolest street (2025).

P.ad: Namba Sennichimae, Chūō-ku, Osaka (between Doguyasuji and Nankai Namba)
P.w: Grid of narrow lanes south of Sennichimae around Sennichi Jizōson-dōri: standing bars, retro izakaya and young owner-run joints from Okinawan to Chinese, plus the bar-packed Misono Building.
Jōdo temple where Tokugawa Ieyasu headquartered during the Sieges of Osaka; famous for its okotsu-butsu Buddhas moulded from the ashes of the dead and accepting remains regardless of sect.

P.n: Abe no Seimei Shrine (安倍晴明神社)
P.w: Shrine on the reputed birthplace of the Heian onmyōji Abe no Seimei, with his statue and 'birth-bath' well; an outlying shrine of Abe Ōji Jinja.
Osaka's 'Ebessan', packed by about a million merchants each 9–11 January for Tōka Ebisu lucky-bamboo; first stop on the Osaka Seven Lucky Gods pilgrimage.

P.ad: Jan Jan Yokochō, Ebisuhigashi, Naniwa-ku, Osaka
P.w: Showa-era smartball parlour in Jan Jan Yokochō — Osaka's only hall dedicated entirely to smartball, running 50+ years.

P.n: Sakai Traditional Crafts Museum (Sakai Densho-kan) — Sakai knives
P.w: Showcase and shop for Sakai's 600-year knife-forging tradition (plus incense, tea and textiles), with live sharpening demos — Sakai is one of Japan's three great cutlery towns.

P.n: Sakai Plaza of Rikyū and Akiko (Sakai Rishō no Mori)
P.ad: Sakai-ku, Sakai, Osaka (facing the site of Sen no Rikyū's residence)
P.w: 2015 museum on Sakai's two icons — tea master Sen no Rikyū and poet Yosano Akiko — with a standing-style (ryūrei) tea service and a tea room facing Rikyū's old house site.

P.n: Nisanzai Kofun (土師ニサンザイ古墳)
P.w: One of the largest keyhole tombs of the UNESCO Mozu-Furuichi group (late 5th c.), its moat-ringed mound a quieter, more photogenic alternative to Nintoku's tomb.
Early-Meiji public park and pine grove on the old western approach to Sumiyoshi Taisha, beside Nankai Sumiyoshi-kōen Station.

P.ad: Tempozan Ferry Landing, 3-2-25 Chikkō, Minato-ku ↔ 3-10-34 Sakurajima, Konohana-ku, Osaka (also Taishō-ku crossings e.g. Senbonmatsu, 1-11-1 Minami-Ongashima)
P.w: Osaka City still runs free public ferries across its harbour rivers; the Tempozan crossing links Kaiyūkan's Minato-ku to Sakurajima (USJ side) — a genuinely local way between the bay sights, with more crossings in Taishō.

P.n: Osaka Nanko Bird Sanctuary (大阪南港野鳥園)
P.ad: Nankō-kita, Suminoe-ku, Osaka (NW corner of Sakishima)
P.w: Free tidal-flat wetland built on Sakishima as a stop-over for migratory shorebirds, with an observation building and tower; closed Wednesdays.

P.ad: Nankō-kita, Suminoe-ku, Osaka (Sakishima, by Trade Center-mae Stn)
P.w: Big waterfront mall/trade complex on Sakishima beside the Cosmo Tower, with harbour-view boardwalks and the Osaka Bay sunset.

P.ad: Kaiyūkan West Pier, Tempozan Harbor Village, Kaigandori, Minato-ku, Osaka
P.w: Sailing-ship replica of Columbus's Santa Maria run by Osaka Suijo Bus, looping Osaka Port from the pier beside Kaiyūkan (day and twilight cruises).
Indoor LEGO attraction (opened 2015) at Tempozan with a Miniland recreating Osaka in bricks, 4D cinema and DUPLO area — for ages 3–10; adults need a child except on adult nights.

One MICHELIN Star French restaurant facing Utsubo Park, cooking seasonal Japanese ingredients in a calm, all-white dining room.
MICHELIN Guide-listed Japanese restaurant in Utsubo pairing seasonal fish with fruit — sweetfish with peach, barracuda with persimmon, Spanish mackerel with apple.
MICHELIN Guide-listed sushi counter tucked into a quiet residential street near Tanimachi, open only at lunchtime.
MICHELIN Guide-listed casual Basque bar in Utsubo for pintxos, tapas and Spanish drinks.
MICHELIN Guide-listed Chinese home cooking in Utsubo; the prix fixe opens with a jiǔ cǎi pén platter influenced by imperial court cuisine.

F.ad: Janjan Yokochō (Nanyo-dori shopping street), Ebisu-higashi, Naniwa-ku, Osaka
F.w: OSAKA-INFO calls Daiko Sushi the famous shop of JanJan Yokochō for rock-bottom-priced sushi; Inside Osaka profiles its two Jan Jan branches ten seconds apart.

F.ad: In front of Tsuruhashi Station, Ikuno-ku, Osaka
F.w: The okonomiyaki chain's flagship by Tsuruhashi Station, a noren-split from the 1950 Tenma Fugetsu (ja.wikipedia); Inside Osaka lists the Tsuruhashi original.
Osaka's best-known craft brewery, a World Beer Awards winner (ja.wikipedia 箕面ブリュワリー); OSAKA-INFO features the brewery's directly-run WAREHOUSE taproom for its exclusive food pairings.
Sakai sweet shop founded in the late Kamakura period (~690 years) whose fifth-generation owner invented kurumi mochi — featured by OSAKA-INFO and Time Out's Sakai guide.
Claims to be Japan's only watarigani-specialist restaurant; reservation-only, three groups a day — in Time Out's 20 must-go restaurants of Southern Osaka and Serai (Shogakukan).

The Hōzenji Yokochō sweet shop that gave Oda Sakunosuke's novel its name — each order of less-sweet zenzai comes split into two bowls, the 'husband and wife'. Inside Osaka places it just beyond the moss-covered Fudō-myōō.

F.n: Kani Doraku Dōtonbori Honten (かに道楽 道頓堀本店)
F.w: The Osaka-born crab house whose giant moving 3D crab sign is one of Dōtonbori's iconic photo spots (Time Out); the honten serves crab course menus.

F.n: Kinryu Ramen Dōtonbori (金龍ラーメン)
F.w: Osaka late-night institution since the early '80s, open 24 hours under its giant dragon sculpture (Time Out); the Aioibashi honten is the chain's flagship (ja.wikipedia).
A century-old Dōtonbori beef house: Time Out calls it legendary for melt-in-the-mouth wagyu sukiyaki and shabu-shabu; ja.wikipedia documents the honten.

F.n: Dōtonbori Kamukura (どうとんぼり神座)
F.w: OSAKA-INFO's 'roots of popular chains' feature sends fans on pilgrimage to Kamukura's Osaka original stores; ja.wikipedia documents the Dōtonbori-born ramen chain and its vegetable-sweet broth.
Osaka's dark-soy 'Osaka Black' ramen specialist; OSAKA-INFO lists the Dōtonbori shop and ja.wikipedia covers the Osaka-founded brand.
Birthplace of Osaka's nikusui — meat udon minus the udon, invented for a hungover Yoshimoto comedian; OSAKA-INFO (2026) and ja.wikipedia's 肉吸い article both credit Chitose.

F.n: Rikuro Ojisan no Mise Namba Honten (りくろーおじさんの店)
F.w: Osaka's beloved fluffy raisin-bottomed cheesecake, branded with the uncle's face and baked to order (OSAKA-INFO, Dec 2025); the Namba shop is the company's honten (ja.wikipedia).

F.n: Takoya Dōtonbori Kukuru Honten (たこ家道頓堀くくる)
F.w: Inside Osaka calls the giant-octopus-signed stall a super-popular Dōtonbori takoyaki stop known for its 'surprise' takoyaki; Time Out: 'the Kukuru chain never disappoints'.
Sister to Portland's Bible Club: a basement pre-Prohibition bar with antique crystal and a deep American/Scotch whisky list (Time Out; 50Best Discovery).

F.ad: B2F Osaka Ekimae Daiichi Building, Umeda, Kita-ku, Osaka, Japan
F.w: Six-seat basement cocktail counter under the Ekimae Daiichi Building run by Ryu Fujii (ex-Bar K); Osaka's first entry on Asia's 50 Best Bars, ranked No. 58 (2025) and No. 72 (2026).

F.ad: Nishishinsaibashi (opposite Triangle Park, Amerikamura), Chuo-ku, Osaka, Japan
F.w: Hidden Amemura cocktail bar behind an Alice-in-Wonderland-sized door marked only by an occult symbol; Asia's 50 Best Bars No. 100 (2025) and No. 70 (2026).

Open-air standing seafood bar outside Kyōbashi Station run by Toyoji Chikumoto since 1992; his flamethrower-seared tuna went viral after Netflix's Street Food: Asia (Osaka, 2019). Four days a week, cash only, queue before 1pm.

F.ad: Shin-Umeda Shokudōgai, Kakudachō, Kita-ku, Osaka, Japan
F.w: Standing takoyaki stall in the Shin-Umeda Shokudōgai warren under JR Osaka Station where locals queue for the negi-mayo balls; picked by Time Out and Inside Osaka.
Udon house founded in 1946 in the middle of the Dōtonbori strip — one of Osaka's most famous noodle specialists, serene inside, known for its dashi and kitsune udon.
Coffee shop and roastery in Kyōmachibori led by World Barista Champion Boram Um; No. 24 on the 2026 World's 100 Best Coffee Shops — the only Osaka entry.
Kissaten founded by Sadao Ibuki in 1934 (Imaike), main store in Sennichimae since 1946 — an Osaka institution for dark-roast drip coffee whose regulars included Kasagi Shizuko and Shofukutei Shokaku.
Flagship of the Osaka okonomiyaki house on the Dōtonbori strip — one of the city's most popular and English-friendly teppan counters; named by Lonely Planet and Inside Osaka.
Noodle house with a 250-year lineage, famous as the home of udon-suki, Osaka's dashi-rich hotpot of udon, seafood and vegetables.

F.n: Misono Kobe (元祖鉄板焼ステーキ みその)
F.w: Founded in Kobe in 1945 by Shigeji Fujioka — the restaurant that invented teppanyaki steak (first grilled for occupation-era American servicemen on a shipyard iron plate) and the counter-teppan format now copied worldwide.
Western-style restaurant founded 1922 where omurice was invented in 1925; the main shop occupies a former tea house with tatami rooms and a garden in Nishi-Shinsaibashi.

F.ad: Nankinmachi, Motomachi-dōri, Chuo-ku, Kobe, Hyōgo, Japan
F.w: Nankinmachi bun shop said to have sold Japan's first butaman (founded 1915); the queue outside is a fixture of Kobe Chinatown.
Confectioner opened on Motomachi-dōri in 1897; its gaufre wafers (1927) are one of the canonical Kobe-born Western sweets of the port city's confectionery culture.

Founded in 1844 and billed as Japan's oldest oden restaurant, now run by the fifth generation; the counter serves kanto-daki oden, the signature saezuri (whale tongue) and sweet-simmered octopus, and was a haunt of writers Oda Sakunosuke and Kaikō Takeshi (Time Out Osaka; GLT/JTB Publishing).

Old-school Sennichimae okonomiyaki house cooking to order; its signboard dish is the suji negiyaki, beef strips and negi in a fluffy batter. Named by Time Out Osaka and Inside Osaka among Namba's okonomiyaki standbys and profiled by Savor Japan.

Dōtonbori okonomiyaki institution run across three generations, with a near-permanent queue; known for its yamaimo-yaki made with a mountain-yam batter (including a vegetarian, gluten-free version) (Inside Osaka; GLT/JTB Publishing).

Near-seventy-year-old okonomiyaki specialist by the Dōtonbori arcade, known for a cabbage-heavy, light batter; order the Ajinoya Mix (pork, squid, octopus, shrimp) or the negiyaki (Inside Osaka; GLT/JTB Publishing).

F.n: Kushinobo Hozenji Honten (串の坊 法善寺本店)
F.ad: Hōzenji area, Namba, Chuo-ku, Osaka, Japan
F.w: Kushikatsu house opened in 1950 by Hōzen-ji, behind a red noren; skewers come with a sauce stewed for over four days from vegetables, chicken bones, sea-bream heads and shrimp (japan-guide Osaka Food Guide; Savor Japan).

F.ad: Jan Jan Yokochō (Nan'yō-dōri), Ebisuhigashi, Naniwa-ku, Osaka
F.w: Jan Jan Yokochō's long-queue kushikatsu counter (founded post-war, 1940s), profiled by Inside Osaka and singled out by Nippon.com as the Shinsekai shop with the longest lines.

F.ad: In front of Tsuruhashi Station, Osaka
F.w: Tsuruhashi's busiest Korean-style yakiniku/horumon house, Time Out's pick for the district and Inside Osaka's 'perpetually busy' recommendation — reserve.
Retro Shinsekai kissaten serving pitch-black coffee, custard pudding and cream soda beneath Tsūtenkaku since 1967 (Time Out); Rurubu flags its 'Purin Royale'.

Sakai confectioner founded in the Enpō era (1673–81) that still makes keshi mochi, the poppy-seed rice cake from the Nanban trade said to be a Sen no Rikyū favourite — in the Sakai city tourism guide and on ja.wikipedia.
Founded 1688; credited as the originator of nikki mochi, cinnamon-laced mochi born of Sakai's Portuguese/Spanish trade era — per ja.wikipedia (肉桂餅) and the Sakai city tourism guide.

Tea merchant founded in Sakai in 1850 — Sen no Rikyū's hometown — whose café serves stone-ground matcha, Rikyū mochi and a tea-cuisine/tea-porridge set; featured by OSAKA-INFO and the Sakai city tourism guide.

F.ad: Wasin Bldg 1F, 4-7 Goryōdōri, Sakai-ku, Sakai, Osaka
F.w: Meat master Tsuneyuki Kobayashi's yakiniku grill near Goryōmae Station, sourcing rare cuts through a private supplier network — Time Out's 20 must-go restaurants of Southern Osaka and a Tabelog Yakiniku WEST Hyakumeiten (2025) selection.

F.ad: 18-1 Kishiki-chō, Kishiwada, Osaka (just south of the Kishiwada Castle moat; 5 min walk from Nankai Takojizō Station)
F.w: 1929–39 magnate's estate on the site of the Kishiwada lords' teahouse, with three tea houses and a stroll garden, now a kaiseki restaurant in private rooms — Time Out's Southern Osaka must-go list and OSAKA-INFO.

F.n: Toretore Ichi (Sakai Dejima Fishing Port market)
F.ad: Sakai Dejima Fishing Port, Sakai-ku, Sakai, Osaka
F.w: Weekend-only fishermen's-association market at Dejima, the old heart of Sakai's anago trade: buy fresh catch and grill it on a rented charcoal grill — OSAKA-INFO and the Sakai city tourism dining guide.

F.ad: 1-23-9 Chiyozaki, Nishi-ku, Osaka (Sakura Bldg 2, 1F; by Kyocera Dome, Dome-mae Chiyozaki / Kujō stns)
F.w: Sri Lankan curry counter by Kyocera Dome that OSAKA-INFO's curry-mania feature names among the pioneers of Osaka's curry scene for spreading the Sri Lankan mix-and-eat style; Tabelog Asia/Ethnic Hyakumeiten 2026.

F.n: Mouriya Honten (モーリヤ本店, Kobe)
F.w: Kobe's oldest beef house (founded 1885); the Sannomiya flagship grills A5 Kobe beef teppanyaki at the counter. Listed in the Kobe Beef council's official restaurant guide (JNTO-hosted) and recommended by Inside Kyoto.

F.n: Steakland Kobe-kan (ステーキランド神戸館)
F.ad: 6F Sannomiya Kogyo Bldg., 1-9-17 Kitanagasa-dori, Chuo-ku, Kobe, Hyogo
F.w: The affordable way into Kobe beef: teppanyaki steak sets (premium tenderloin with soup, salad, veg, dessert and coffee) a minute from Hankyu Sannomiya. Named in the official Kobe Beef restaurant guide and by Inside Kyoto.

F.ad: 1F Hillside Terrace, 1-22-13 Nakayamate-dori, Chuo-ku, Kobe, Hyogo
F.w: Kitano-chō teppanyaki house where chefs grill Kobe beef with butter and garlic before you; Inside Kyoto calls it one of the best places in Kobe to try the city's wagyu, and it is listed in the official Kobe Beef restaurant guide.

F.n: Freundlieb (フロインドリーブ, Kobe)
F.w: German bakery founded by Heinrich Freundlieb in 1924, since 1997 housed in the W.M. Vories-designed former Kobe Union Church: cakes, sandwiches and pastries under a vaulted nave.

F.n: Nishimura Coffee Nakayamate Honten (にしむら珈琲店 中山手本店)
F.w: Kobe's landmark coffee house since 1948 and one of the first in the city to serve cappuccino and Vienna coffee; on-site roasting and cakes at the Nakayamate main shop.
The shop that put Wakayama ramen on the national map when it won TV Tokyo's 'Japan's best ramen' battle in 1998; porky tonkotsu-shōyu chūka soba, eaten with self-serve hayazushi mackerel sushi.

F.n: Mitsumori Honpo (三津森本舗, Arima Onsen)
F.w: The original maker of Arima's tansan senbei — 1 mm wafers baked by hand with the town's carbonated spring water — on the main Yumotozaka street; the adjoining Mitsumori Cafe serves senbei French toast.

F.n: Ichiju Nisai Ueno Minoten (一汁二菜うえの 箕面店)
F.w: Michelin-listed (2026 guide) Japanese restaurant at the foot of the Minoh mountains, near the Minoo Park trailhead.
